<reason>Side A (CON) ran a vivid, disciplined campaign: the "morgue on Saturday night" vignette, the concession-extracting Q1 (cameras interrupt zero lethal behaviors pre-crash), the owner-liability trap, and the sharp "outliers vs. corridor average" responsiveness point that B never answered head-on. A's rebuttals were the sharpest in the debate and its A1/A2 answers were direct. But B (PRO) held the stronger overall path: the speed-severity mechanism ("even CON's drunk kills by physics, not blood-alchemy") blunted A's flagship vignette; the coverage/capacity and opportunity-cost asymmetry went essentially unrebutted; and on externalities B clearly won—showing stops share every fee harm while adding armed encounters and profiling, and landing the decisive framing that CON's own reform package concedes stops' harms are structural. B answered both pressure questions honestly (designate-the-driver, severity-in-every-crash). Costs for B: a clipped opening, somewhat repetitive severity restatements, and a closing claim that CON "never showed" marginal yield despite A4.1 having answered it. A's unaddressed migration-to-side-streets point and responsiveness challenge keep this competitive, but B wins the conjunction the motion actually asks about, narrowly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Pressure Q1 forced B to concede cameras detect no impairment, distraction, or belt use—then A's Rebuttal 2 pressed the wound: "PRO's mechanism works best on the drivers least likely to die." B's recovery ("even the drunk kills by velocity, and lower corridor speeds shrink lethality of every crash type") was the debate's decisive exchange, converting a concession into a stronger universal-mechanism claim that A's closing "outliers" point dented but never broke.</best_rebuttal>
